title: Clickable Brain Atlas
description: A stylized, procedurally drawn human brain shown in a lateral (side) view and a midsagittal (midline cut) view. Students hover to highlight regions and click to read each structure's main jobs, the effects of damage, and a Brain Bee fact. A quiz mode names a structure and checks whether the student clicks the correct region.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: Neuroscience
Neuroanatomy
Cerebral Cortex
Brainstem
Localization of Function
learningObjectives: Identify 19 major brain structures and landmarks in a lateral view and a midsagittal view, scoring at least 80% in quiz mode in each view.
Recall one main job and one effect of damage for each of the lobes, the deep structures, and the three parts of the brainstem.
prerequisites: Anatomical directions and the sagittal plane (Chapter 4, Section 4.2)
keyQuestions: Which groove separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe, and what kinds of cortex lie on each side of it?
Which structure connects the left and right hemispheres, and where does it sit in a midsagittal view?
What are the three parts of the brainstem from top to bottom, and which one controls breathing and heart rate?
Why does damage to one cerebellar hemisphere affect the same side of the body?
misconceptions: The cerebellum is a small, unimportant part of the brain (it holds roughly 80% of the brain's neurons).
Each hemisphere controls the same side of the body (the cerebrum works contralaterally; only the cerebellum works on the same side).
The prefrontal cortex is separate from the frontal lobe (it is the front part of the frontal lobe).
The thalamus relays every sense (smell is the exception).
modelAssumptions: Region shapes are stylized polygons placed in their correct anatomical positions; sizes and outlines are simplified.
The lateral view shows the left hemisphere with the front of the head facing left.
Lobe boundaries without a real groove (frontal-prefrontal, parietal-occipital, temporal-parietal) are drawn as dashed imaginary lines.
limitations: Deep structures such as the hippocampus, amygdala, basal ganglia, insula, and lateral ventricles are not drawn.
The midsagittal view shows the fourth ventricle but not the third ventricle or cerebral aqueduct.
